subject: anaesthesia
title: Paediatric Anaesthesia: Airway Anatomy, Neonatal Physiology, and Laryngospasm

steps.title: Paediatric Anatomical Airway Differences
steps.tx: **Paediatric upper airway anatomical differences** create distinct intubation challenges: young children possess a disproportionately large prominent occiput (flexing the neck when supine, requiring a shoulder roll rather than head ring), a relatively massive tongue filling the oral cavity, a high cephalad larynx positioned at the C3-C4 vertebral level (compared to C4-C6 in adults), and a narrow, stiff, omega-shaped epiglottis projecting at 45 degrees.

steps.title: Funnel-Shaped Larynx and Cricoid Ring
steps.tx: **Subglottic funnel-shaped infant larynx** narrows progressively toward the non-distensible complete ring of the cricoid cartilage. Whereas the vocal cords represent the narrowest anatomical constriction in adults, the subglottic cricoid ring forms the narrowest functional airway passage in neonates and infants. Because airway resistance is inversely proportional to radius to the fourth power (Poiseuille law), 1 millimeter of subglottic circumferential edema reduces cross-sectional airway area by 75 percent.

left.title: Adult Cylindrical Larynx
points: Vocal cord glottic opening is narrowest anatomical aperture
One millimeter mucosal edema causes negligible airway obstruction
Larynx displays cylindrical straight-walled architectural contour

right.title: Infant Funnel-Shaped Larynx
points: Subglottic cricoid cartilage ring forms narrowest constriction
One millimeter circumferential edema slashes airway lumen area by 75%
Produces severe inspiratory stridor and respiratory failure

steps.title: Endotracheal Tube Formulas for Children
steps.tx: **Paediatric endotracheal tube sizing formulas** calculate appropriate internal diameter (ID) in millimeters: for uncuffed tubes, size equals (Age in years divided by 4) plus 4. For modern low-pressure microcuffed tubes, size equals (Age in years divided by 4) plus 3.5. Depth of insertion at the central incisors in centimeters is calculated as (Age in years divided by 2) plus 12, or roughly three times the tube internal diameter.

steps.title: Neonatal Cardiovascular Physiology
steps.tx: **Neonatal rate-dependent cardiac output** results from immature myocardial ultrastructure: neonatal cardiomyocytes possess fewer myofibrils organized in a disorganized non-compliant matrix, leaving the left ventricle with minimal stroke volume reserve. Consequently, neonates cannot increase cardiac output by augmenting stroke volume (Starling curve is flat); cardiac output depends almost entirely on heart rate, meaning bradycardia (heart rate under 100 bpm) triggers severe circulatory shock.

left.title: Neonatal Myocardial Mechanics
points: Non-compliant, stiff ventricular chambers with minimal stretch
Stroke volume is fixed; cardiac output is strictly heart-rate dependent
Profound cardiac collapse occurs when heart rate falls below 80 to 100 bpm

right.title: Mature Adult Myocardial Mechanics
points: Distensible ventricular myocardium with robust Frank-Starling reserve
Augments stroke volume to compensate for moderate bradycardia
Maintains normal cardiac output across wide heart rate ranges

steps.title: Fast Alveolar Induction Kinetics
steps.tx: **Rapid inhalational induction kinetics in children** stem from unique cardiorespiratory physiology: children possess an exceptionally high ratio of alveolar minute ventilation to functional residual capacity (5:1 in infants, compared to 1.5:1 in adults), alongside a high cardiac output directed primarily to the vessel-rich organ group. This rapidly elevates alveolar volatile anaesthetic concentrations toward inspired concentrations (FA/FI), producing induction and overdose twice as fast as in adults.

steps.title: Paediatric Preoperative Fasting Guidelines
steps.tx: **Pediatric fasting consensus guidelines** balance dehydration prevention against aspiration risk: clear liquids (water, clear apple juice without pulp, oral electrolyte solutions) are permitted up to two hours prior to surgery; human breast milk requires four hours of fasting; infant formula requires six hours; and light non-fat meals require six hours. Chewing gum and sweets are withheld for two hours.

steps.title: Retinopathy and Apnoea of Prematurity
steps.tx: **Prematurity-specific anaesthetic hazards** include apnoea of prematurity (central and obstructive pauses in breathing occurring postoperatively in infants under 60 weeks post-conceptual age, demanding overnight hospital apnea monitoring). In addition, unmonitored hyperoxaemia in premature infants triggers retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), wherein high PaO2 causes retinal arteriolar vasoconstriction and vaso-obliteration, mandating tight oxygen saturation targets of 91 to 95 percent.

left.title: Apnoea of Prematurity Vulnerability
points: Post-conceptual age under 60 weeks carries high risk
Recurrent central apnoea emerges in first 12 hours post-surgery
Requires 24 hours of inpatient continuous pulse oximetry monitoring

right.title: Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP)
points: Hyperoxia (SpO2 >95% or PaO2 >80 mmHg) triggers retinal vessel obliteration
Rebound neovascularization causes retinal detachment and blindness
Target SpO2 strictly between 91 and 95 percent in premature infants

steps.title: Paediatric Laryngospasm and Bradycardia
steps.tx: **Pediatric laryngospasm reflex and bradycardia** occur with high frequency during airway instrumentation under light anaesthesia, exacerbated by copious respiratory secretions or blood in the pharynx. Because hypoxaemia triggers profound vagal bradycardia in young children, acute laryngospasm rapidly progresses to hypoxemic cardiac arrest, mandating gentle pharyngeal suctioning, positive-pressure oxygen, and intravenous atropine with succinylcholine.
